artworks.title: Landscape with Hypsipyle and Opheltes
artworks.description: Reinhart's Karlsruhe landscape sets the infant Opheltes with his nurse Hypsipyle in a Nemean wilderness — the quiet before the serpent strike that Amphiaraus will rename Archemorus, 'Beginning of Doom,' and that founds the Nemean Games.

artworks.title: Hypsipyle Finds Opheltes Killed by a Snake
artworks.description: Becker's Neues Museum mural (surviving in reproduction) stages the discovery: Opheltes slain by the Nemean serpent while Hypsipyle guided the Seven to water. The infant's death is the aetiology of the games held in his honour.

artworks.title: Opheltes (small bronze)
artworks.description: A small bronze from the Archaeological Museum of Nemea identified with the hero Opheltes — the infant whose heroon and games made Nemea a Panhellenic sanctuary. Cult objects keep Archemorus present where the Seven paused on the road to Thebes.

artworks.title: Opheltes Ensnared by the Snake
artworks.description: A handbook reconstruction after an ancient relief shows the infant Archemorus in the serpent's coils — the visual type of Opheltes' death that modern archaeology still cites beside the Nemean shrine.

popCulture.title: Nemean Games
popCulture.description: Funeral games for Opheltes/Archemorus become the Nemean Games — the infant's death as the origin story of one of the four Panhellenic festivals.

popCulture.title: Opheltes
popCulture.description: Son of Lycurgus of Nemea, nursed by Hypsipyle, killed by a serpent — renamed Archemorus by Amphiaraus as an omen of the Seven's doom.
